A semitone is the small pitch step from one fret to its neighbour; twelve semitones form an octave.

messages.52e516dd5a100df9: A 4/4 bar has four quarter beats. A note can ring across counts without another attack; a rest requires silence while counting. Gently touch the sounding string to stop it without striking the body or pressing it to a fret. Tempo is the speed of the beat. BPM means beats per minute; in these 4/4 tasks, each beat is a quarter note. If you use an available external metronome, let one click match each spoken number: 1, 2, 3, 4. At 60 BPM, clicks are one second apart; this is an example, not a required playing speed. Choose a pace at which you can prepare the next action without rushing.
messages.35e7e36a2d025be2: On E play open, fret 1, open, fret 3 with a pause between attempts. Then A open/fret 2, then D open/fret 2. Speak string/fret and sounding name. Mute the previous note before switching. Then isolate a fretted ending: on string 3 fret 2, pluck B1 on count 1, let it ring through 2, stop on 3 and count 3–4 in silence. Ease the fretting pressure while keeping light finger contact on the string; gentle contact from a plucking finger can also stop it. Keep the other strings quiet. The intended sequence is B1 then silence, with no open A between them. Repeat on string 2 fret 2, E2 then silence, only after the first ending is clear.
messages.7324997aef8f187b: If reaching 3 strains, isolate open/1 first or shift rather than stretch. If pitch seems uncertain, separate fretting placement from external tuning; the app does not judge either. If an open A or D appears as you stop the fretted note, repeat just that ending without a pulse: stop the string with a gentle plucking-hand touch, release fretting pressure while retaining light contact, then move away only after the string is quiet. Avoid pulling the string sideways. Return to the counted B1-to-silence bar and compare the same ending.
messages.4f37f8d8a67da9f6: Choose and write a comfortable tempo. Isolate bars 3–4 root/fifth changes, then 5–6 eighths, then 7 octave crossing. At bar 8 stop on beat 3 and count through 4. Practise pairs with one silent count-in bar; connect only after reading the events. If you use an available external metronome for the comparison, write its setting as “quarter note = ___ BPM” and keep that setting for both full attempts. Count 1 2 3 4 with its four clicks before starting; place each “and” halfway between clicks, without doubling the click setting for eighth notes. If you change the tempo, begin a new pair of attempts at that setting. The click supplies a reference; it does not judge your playing.
messages.f337d688fa8aa86f: Black keys repeat in groups of two and three. C is the white key immediately left of a pair. Moving right raises pitch; moving left lowers it. White keys repeat C D E F G A B (Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Si). Neighbouring black or white keys are one semitone apart. A sharp (♯) raises a named note by one semitone; a flat (♭) lowers it. The black key between C and D can be called C♯ or D♭: two names for the same piano key. E–F and B–C have no black key between them; sharps and flats can also name white keys. These written studies use natural white-key notes.
messages.198073a51153e5ec: Find two C keys within C3–G4; an optional third C only if your keyboard has it. Name C through B in one octave, then reverse. Find a C and the D immediately to its right. Point to the black key between them: say “C sharp” and “D flat”, and check that both names point to that one key. Use relative names here; lesson 3 establishes the octave register.
messages.b4683b73a429bb93: Both hands: thumb 1, index 2, middle 3, ring 4, little 5. Let fingers curve naturally; wrists stay mobile, not locked. Press then release one key; avoid forcing a fixed hand shape. Before playing C4, use the keyboard diagram below. On an 88-key piano, middle C is the fourth C from the left (white key number 24, overall key number 40); the first key is A0. On shorter keyboards, consult the manufacturer’s key map for middle C / MIDI note 60. Manufacturers may label this C3, C4 or C5. Do not choose a C only because it looks central. If the map is unavailable, register identification is uncertain: practise relative note direction without calling a key C4 or claiming the required range. On an electronic keyboard, use its manual to check that transpose and octave-shift settings are zero before comparing sounding pitches with these labels. If you cannot confirm the settings, mark the sounding register uncertain and continue only the relative-key tasks.
messages.fa05321572c9d296: In 4/4 count 1 2 3 4. A quarter note lasts one beat, half note two, whole note four. A rest is counted silence, not an extra pause. Tempo is beats per minute; choose a comfortable slow pulse, not a pass threshold. The upper 4 means four beats in each bar; the lower 4 makes the quarter note the counting unit. A bar line starts the next group at 1 without adding silence.
messages.7205dd528c86813f: Clap on beats 1, 2, 3, 4. Then clap on 1, count and wait on 2; clap on 3, count and wait on 4. A clap is a brief onset, not a sound you hold. Next clap on 1, stay silent on 2, clap 3 and 4. After locating middle C in lesson 3, play C4 on 1 and keep its key down while counting 2; release and play on 3, hold through 4. These are two actual half notes. Repeat twice. Before each new attempt, count one silent 1 2 3 4 to prepare. While linking bars, go straight from 4 to the next 1 without another preparation bar. Let the final held note last its full counted duration before releasing.
messages.26c840b0ae3e180d: Legato connects notes with controlled release; do not keep every key down. A slur groups a phrase; a tie joins the same pitch across durations. p is soft, f loud, crescendo gradually louder. Keep volume comfortable, no forced impact. For electronic keyboards, touch response must be available and enabled for your touch to change loudness. Keep the master volume comfortable and fixed during the comparison. If two comfortable touches give the same loudness, check the manual rather than striking harder; fixed-velocity settings or a keyboard without touch response can prevent this task from producing a contrast.
messages.fa85424fbab93bdc: If keys overlap into a blur, practise two notes and release the first as the next starts. Pedal stays off. If your keyboard cannot vary loudness with touch, practise the note connections at one comfortable volume and record “dynamic contrast not assessed on this keyboard.” That device limitation is not evidence of a playing mistake.
messages.1e5299382f410392: Pitch means how high or low a tone sounds; volume means how loud it is. A nearby higher tone need not be louder. This course first uses relative directions, not fixed semitone intervals or accuracy scores. Work within a small, easy part of your voice; avoid testing your range limits.
messages.677967f6df093670: The study uses eight equal half-beat cells per 4/4 bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”: each number is a beat and each “and” is halfway to the next number. V starts the stated tone/syllable; = adds no new start and continues current sound or silence; R releases sound and counts silence. = never means hold your breath. Normal breathing is allowed during rests and whenever needed. Written durations are suggestions, not physiological targets. H remains the higher-tone label; it is never the continuation symbol.
messages.d6254c4d29708317: First tap four even beats without singing; then count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” with eight evenly spaced taps. On the study, tap only each printed V while the half-beat count continues through = and R. Inspect the full silent bars 6 and 8 and the silent endings of bars 1–4 before singing. Choose a tempo and span that allow an easy short phrase, or shorten the voiced part and label your exact adapted task.
messages.3a07e98e6bc528fb: Original contour in quarter-note beats. M = your comfortable centre; L/H = nearby lower/higher, not quieter/louder. Each letter starts a new sound. R = counted silence. No fixed note or interval.
messages.a754540dab413bd4: A semitone is the nearest key to the right or left, black or white. A sharp ♯ raises a note by one semitone: F♯ is the black key right of F. A flat ♭ lowers it: B♭ is the black key left of B. One black key has two names, so F♯ and G♭ share a key. A natural ♮ cancels a sharp or flat. E–F and B–C are semitones with no black key between them.
messages.86ceb2d75dba4c7a: With right finger 2, touch C4 then each next semitone up to C5, naming each key aloud with a sharp name. Return down naming flats. Then play F4 F♯4 G4 and B4 B♭4 A4 slowly with relaxed fingers. A sign lasts until the end of its bar unless a natural cancels it.
messages.5ed7b20c3f870697: Can I name both possible names of a black key and find E–F and B–C?
messages.65dd6df344fd7bde: If names mix up, go back to lesson 2 and find the two-black-key groups first; then move one semitone at a time and say the direction before the name.
messages.cdf0e3b946b8249b: Intervals from a second to a fifth
messages.3863f3d4ccbd12e6: An interval counts letter names from one note to another, including both. C to D is a second (line to space), C to E a third (line to line or space to space), C to F a fourth, C to G a fifth. On the staff a second moves to the next position; a third skips one position; a fifth skips three. In a five-finger position the finger difference plus one gives the interval.
messages.776bca9c83f16de0: In right-hand C position play C4–D4, C4–E4, C4–F4, C4–G4, naming each interval before playing. Then read these pairs from the staff in your head first: E4–G4, D4–G4, F4–G4, C4–F4. Name, play, and compare only afterwards. Repeat with left hand C3–G3.
messages.708d23bb9cb91747: Can I name an interval from the staff before I play it?
messages.3525b5176c08b942: If counting slips, count letter names on your fingers including the first note, then check line/space pattern; a third always stays line–line or space–space.
messages.9e85464c23d40c92: G position and moving the hand
messages.4ab43466293ab742: A five-finger position is named by the lowest note it covers. In right-hand G position, fingers 1–5 cover G4 A4 B4 C5 D5. In left-hand G position, fingers 5–1 cover G2 A2 B2 C3 D3. Moving position means lifting the whole hand during a rest or a held note, not stretching one finger. G major uses F♯; when a melody meets F, play the black key F♯ unless a natural is written.
messages.9f905221bfd1ab14: Right hand: play C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 in C position, rest one beat while moving finger 1 to G4, then play G4 A4 B4 C5 D5. Then play this G-position phrase: G4 A4 B4 G4 | A4 F♯4 G4 half. F♯ is reached with finger 1 moving one key left of G or with a short shift; choose the comfortable option and keep the shoulder low.
messages.f35c11b312bcb56f: Can I move to a new position during a rest without rushing the count?
messages.21fd7214f6a4f236: If the move is late, practise only the last note, the rest and the first note of the new position, counting aloud; place the hand silently before playing.
messages.59237ad37ed88220: C major scale with a thumb crossing
messages.b6cf3e3e399d6168: A scale is a stepwise order of notes. C major uses only white keys: C D E F G A B C. One octave in the right hand is fingered 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5: after finger 3 plays E, the thumb passes under to F. Descending, finger 3 crosses over the thumb from F to E. The left hand ascends 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1: finger 3 crosses over to A. Keep the wrist level and let the arm travel.
messages.fe720e863354f060: First practise only the crossing: right E4 (3) to F4 (1) and back, slowly ten times with a release between. Then play C4 to C5 and back, one note per beat at a slow tempo. Left hand alone: C3 to C4 and back with 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1. Hands together only if each hand is even.
messages.de4bb27f570f9bd8: Is the crossing note as even in time as its neighbours?
messages.535751df7e784310: If the thumb bumps or the elbow lifts, slow down and play only three notes around the crossing; let the elbow move sideways with the hand.
messages.805e1f1d379f4d4a: In 3/4 each bar has three quarter-note beats, counted 1 2 3, with beat 1 slightly stronger. A dot adds half of a note's value: a dotted half lasts three beats, a dotted quarter lasts one and a half. A dotted quarter is often followed by an eighth: count 1 (2) and | the eighth falls on the 'and' of beat 2.
messages.8d69e8924b2c429a: Clap and count before playing. 3/4: C4 E4 G4 | C5 dotted half | G4 E4 C4 | dotted half C4. 4/4 with dotted rhythm: C4 dotted quarter, D4 eighth, E4 half | E4 dotted quarter, D4 eighth, C4 half. Then play each line with the right hand in C position, counting aloud.
messages.10c933c82dac1fd9: Does each bar add up to its time signature without an extra or missing beat?
messages.35d3a3b7f0cc030c: If the dotted rhythm becomes even, count in eighths (1 and 2 and) and hold the dotted note through three of them before the short note.
messages.9ec374ca939d23ae: Legato connects notes: release one key exactly as the next sounds. Staccato, a dot above or below the notehead, means short and detached; the key rises quickly but the beat keeps its full length. An accent > asks for one note a little stronger than its neighbours. These are touch choices, not force; keep the hand loose.
messages.71943ef7f39a6c08: Play C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 three ways at the same slow tempo: all legato, all staccato, then legato with an accent on each beat 1. Then play G4 F4 E4 D4 C4 with the first two staccato and the last three legato. Listen for silence between staccato notes while the count continues.
messages.93b7ec2ee4592433: Can I keep the same tempo while changing only the touch?
messages.6cd83c66f224a002: If staccato speeds you up, tap the pulse with the other hand or foot and play staccato only on every other beat first.
messages.160358f6a645d612: Left-hand C, F and G7 chords
messages.d1141237f38f676a: In C major the main chords are I (C), IV (F) and V7 (G7). A close left-hand pattern avoids big jumps: C chord C3 E3 G3 with fingers 5 3 1; F chord C3 F3 A3 with 5 2 1; G7 chord B2 F3 G3 with 5 2 1. C stays as a shared note between C and F; G stays between C and G7. Shared notes let the hand change with small finger moves.
messages.1f50f76c99ce8b60: Left hand alone, one chord per bar as a whole note: C | F | C | G7 | C. Move only the fingers that change. Then accompany this original right-hand melody in C position: E4 G4 E4 C4 | D4 F4 D4 G4 | F4 E4 D4 half | C4 whole, with left chords C | G7 | G7 | C held for each bar.
messages.0c1a29254dedde0c: Can I change chords on beat 1 while the melody keeps its rhythm?
messages.ea116dc6ee05593d: If the change is late, play only the last melody note and the new chord together several times; then add one bar before it.
messages.490614841162cad1: Map a new piece on your own
messages.8d261103d932a69e: Independent practice starts before playing. Choose a short beginner piece you are allowed to use, or write your own eight bars in C or G. Map it on paper: key and sharps/flats, time signature, the hand positions and where they move, the hardest two bars, and any dynamics or touch marks. A map turns a page into small, ordered tasks.
messages.43cc72bd172837f5: Write your map in five lines. Then choose the order: the hardest bars first, hands separately, slowly; then connect bars in pairs. Set a starting tempo you can keep without stopping. Do not look for a recording of the piece as a requirement; reading and counting are the goal here.
messages.1c9310a2f4830c55: Could someone else follow my map to know what to practise first?
messages.dcff1d74c6a56442: If the piece feels too hard, choose fewer bars or a piece in one position; a smaller complete map is better than a long unfinished one.
messages.e16983bda4075814: A practice cycle has four parts: a short warm-up (lesson 19 scale or lesson 17 intervals), focused work on one mapped problem, a full play-through at the chosen tempo, and a note for next time. Short regular sessions usually help more than one long session. Rest when hands or shoulders feel tense.
messages.4f1638d7333b40e0: On one day run the cycle with your lesson 23 piece: warm-up, one focus task, one play-through, one written note (bar, count, observed result). On another day repeat the same play-through at the same tempo and compare that bar: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Then write the next focus and, only if comfortable, a slightly faster tempo.
messages.e065f82a12230967: Can I plan, run and compare a practice session without the course telling me each step?
messages.b60097bd280717ba: If a session goes badly, shorten it to the warm-up and one bar; a finished small cycle still counts. A teacher can help with individual technique.
messages.c92f6f6432039d7d: Review key direction and C locations, finger numbers, both clef anchors and durations, sharps and flats, intervals, G position, the C major scale, 3/4 and dotted rhythms, touch marks and the left-hand C, F and G7 chords. Perform lesson 15, decode lesson 14 afresh and run one cycle with your own mapped piece from lessons 23–24. Your own observation is not a sensor result or mastery certificate. This is a bounded beginner foundation, not grade equivalence or complete piano training.
messages.be9753e94bc7af47: On separate days, try naming/reading, steady counting, the two-hand study and your own piece. For each outcome, write one of “observed”, “needs another attempt”, or “uncertain”: find a C and name its white and black neighbours, including a sharp and a flat name (2–3, 16); explain 4/4 and 3/4 and count a note–rest bar and a dotted rhythm without adding a beat (4, 8, 20); name an interval from the staff before playing (17); move to G position during a rest (18); play the C major scale with an even thumb crossing (19); change left-hand chords on beat 1 under a melody (22); keep melody and bass durations in the four-bar study (10–12, 15); and map a new piece, run your own cycle and compare one smaller correction at the same tempo (23–24). “No observed error” is also valid; it is not proof of mastery. Revisit the matching lesson when uncertain. A device-limited dynamics check stays unassessed (13). A teacher can help with individual technique and notation.
messages.62570b2cbf85acb4: Locate and name keys including sharps and flats; count notes, rests, 3/4 and dotted rhythms; read both clefs and intervals; play each hand, G position, the C major scale, a two-hand study and left-hand I–IV–V7 accompaniment; then map a new piece and run your own practice cycle with one specific correction. All checks are self-observation.
messages.8991b3e5a178cc23: Five small steps up and down
messages.0f655763bb42b5ed: Extend the L/M/H idea into a short stair: number five small, even-feeling steps 1 2 3 4 5, starting from a comfortable low tone near your L. Each step only moves a little higher than the one before. This is a personal relative pattern; exact interval sizes, a key or a note name are not checked. Keep volume the same on every step.
messages.032ef6620567271d: Hum 1 2 3 2 1 slowly, one quarter count each, then rest a bar. If comfortable, hum 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 1. Write which step felt least easy, or “uncertain”. If the top step strains, stop at 3 and keep that smaller stair.
messages.761dcf140515f81b: Can I go up and back down by small steps without getting louder at the top?
messages.1cd74350a528ac72: If steps blur, speak the numbers on one tone first, then hum only 1 2 1 and 2 3 2; a smaller stair is a valid choice.
messages.d92355c3260e7411: A skip leaves out a step: 1 3 means moving from step 1 to step 3 without singing 2. Returning to 1 after a skip helps you check that your home tone stayed the same. Think the missing step silently if it helps. Accuracy is not measured here; you compare by your own listening.
messages.3270b663e016e316: Hum 1 2 3 then 1 3, with a rest between. Then try 1 3 1 and 3 5 3 if your five-step stair was comfortable. Read this contour silently first, then hum it: 1 3 2 1 | 3 5 3 R. Each number is one quarter count; R is a counted silence.
messages.acdab0331d9759e9: After a skip, does my return to 1 feel like the same home tone?
messages.754b48448a7cea71: If the skip lands unclear, sing the full steps 1 2 3, then repeat 1 3 while thinking 2; record “uncertain” rather than guessing.
messages.5128c50eda0774c7: A crescendo < grows gradually louder; a diminuendo > fades gradually softer. Volume and pitch are separate: a crescendo on one tone stays on the same tone. Stay inside a comfortable range of loudness; louder never means pushing the throat. Breath support for a phrase comes from an easy inhale, not a forced one.
messages.4b843f9b3b1c49f4: On a comfortable hum of M, count four beats: grow a little on 1–2, fade on 3–4, then rest a bar. Then speak “one two three four” with the same shape. Finally hum the 1 2 3 2 1 stair with a gentle crescendo up and diminuendo down, keeping the top step no louder than easy speech.
messages.185d76f4f69bc6d6: Can I change loudness gradually while the tone stays easy?
messages.53c09000bc03d5d9: If the throat tightens, return to speaking volume and practise only the fade; a smaller range of loudness is fine.
messages.59bd1f06d46ddaa8: Your own warm-up and stop signals
messages.889666cf65b14974: A warm-up prepares, it does not test. Build a short order from earlier lessons: settle and breathe (2–3), a gentle hum (4), short starts and releases (5), a small stair (16). Keep it about five minutes. Stop signals: pain, hoarseness that lasts, a scratchy throat, breathlessness or dizziness. Then rest; lasting voice problems need a qualified professional. This course gives no medical advice.
messages.ca31d1a7355c28a4: Write your warm-up as four lines with a time for each. Try it once today. Afterwards write one word for how the voice felt (easy / effortful / uncertain) and one change for next time. Water and short breaks are allowed at any point.
messages.ae04bb7e06d890b4: Do I know my warm-up order and when I must stop?
messages.19411f0439194991: If a warm-up step feels effortful, remove it and keep the breath and hum only; a shorter warm-up is still a warm-up.
messages.43e5a07f899ecf51: Map a short melody you choose
messages.dfd4878b9476a695: Choose a short melody you already know and may sing for yourself, such as a traditional children's tune, or write your own four bars with the contour symbols. Do not copy song lyrics into notes you share. Map it: where phrases end, where you will breathe, which part goes highest, and a relative contour using L M H or steps 1–5. A map makes the melody practisable in small parts.
messages.311416906795ecce: Write the map in four lines: phrases, breath marks, highest part, contour. Speak the words or a neutral syllable in rhythm first. Then hum one phrase at a time, resting between phrases. If the highest part strains, choose a lower starting tone or keep that phrase spoken.
messages.e0caaf76b57f00b6: Can I show where each phrase breathes and where the melody goes highest?
messages.8717ec23793163b4: If the melody is too long, map only its first phrase; a short complete map is better than a long guess.
messages.561b9522aad27503: An independent session has four parts: your warm-up (19), one focus from your map (20), one comfortable run of the melody, and a written note. Short, regular sessions usually help more than long ones. Comfort decides the length; stopping is always a valid result.
messages.f90bafc885751253: Run the cycle once with your lesson 20 melody and write: focus, observed result for one phrase (late breath / unclear word / effort / no observed issue / uncertain). On another day repeat the same run and compare that phrase: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Write the next focus.
messages.039097afdc8e9dbc: Can I plan, run and compare a practice session on my own?
messages.e0b0f6a435d94f54: If a session feels effortful, end it after the warm-up and note that; a teacher can help with individual technique and choosing a comfortable range.
messages.136d13a42e8e261c: Review comfortable start/stop choices, natural breathing, short hum/onset/release, counted rests, pitch versus volume, three-tone contour, the five-step stair and skips, gradual loudness changes, vowels, original words, phrase planning, your own warm-up and stop signals, and the melody you mapped. This bounded written foundation does not certify range, intonation, sustained-note quality, vibrato, health or a voice type.
messages.5c6790eb47d87eb0: On another comfortable day, before reopening the explanations, recall what M/L/H, R and = mean, name your warm-up order and two reasons to stop vocalizing. Check your answer against lessons 8, 13 and 19 and return to a missed item. Decode the two-bar contour before revealing its reading answer, hum the small stair only if comfortable, and run one practice cycle with your mapped melody (lessons 20–21), comparing one phrase with your earlier note. Name one repeatable outcome and one uncertainty. Rest is always a valid choice.
messages.2d9e2ecd218e808c: Explain and attempt comfortable short onset/release, natural breath without holding, counted rhythm/rests, a small personal pitch contour and five-step stair distinct from volume, gradual loudness changes, vowels/clear original words and an original/adapted eight-bar study; build your own warm-up with stop signals, map a short melody you choose and run your own practice cycle with another-day comparison. Self-observation and reading only; no audio/health/range/intonation/mastery verification.
messages.00505c2ab9c65cc3: Written in 4→1 string order, G is 0232: index 1 on string 3 fret 2, middle 2 on string 1 fret 2, ring 3 on string 2 fret 3; string 4 open. Em is 0432: ring 3 on string 3 fret 4, middle 2 on string 2 fret 3, index 1 on string 1 fret 2. G and Em share the notes G and B. A comfortable alternative Em is 0402 if the full shape is too wide.
messages.1a29082eeeeb83ac: Form G, pluck each string separately, then strum gently four downstrokes. Do the same for Em. Then change G | Em | G | Em, one bar each, strumming on beat 1 and letting it ring, forming the next chord during beat 4.
messages.89bacf166cc822f3: Does every string of G and Em sound clearly before I add rhythm?
messages.4c8adfd90d26884d: If a string is muted, pluck strings one at a time and adjust the finger touching it; arch the finger and place it just behind the fret wire.
messages.6872393d89e88dce: Dm is 2210: middle 2 on string 4 fret 2, ring 3 on string 3 fret 2, index 1 on string 2 fret 1; string 1 open. A7 is 0100: index 1 on string 3 fret 1, other strings open. In the key of F, F, Dm and C belong together; A7 leads well into Dm. Notice that F (2010) and Dm (2210) differ by one finger.
messages.bcd70f421cda3a53: Change F → Dm by adding one finger, back and forth slowly. Then play A7 → Dm. Then the loop F | Dm | A7 | Dm, one bar each with four downstrokes, keeping fingers that stay in place on the strings.
messages.4e073202db4f5487: Can I keep the shared finger down when changing F to Dm?
messages.26814232676a1a46: If Dm buzzes, check that the index on fret 1 is close to the fret wire and the ring finger does not touch string 2.
messages.de19d769e57c1f2d: A common strum and a waltz strum
messages.df507592eb043c6d: A strum pattern places D and U in the eight half-beat slots of a bar. A common pattern is D, D U, U D U: slots D · D U · U D U, with no stroke on the 'and' of 1 and on beat 3. Keep the hand moving down and up all the time; only touch the strings where a stroke is written. In 3/4 a simple waltz strum is D D D or D D U D U.
messages.af944b6a9df595b7: On a muted strum (left hand resting lightly on the strings), count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & and play D · D U · U D U for four bars. Then play it on C. Then on C | Am | F | G7. For 3/4, play D D U D U on C | G | G | C, counting 1 & 2 & 3 &.
messages.fa0b2980d7414d9e: Does my hand keep moving evenly even where there is no stroke?
messages.8d69bad37a0e819b: If the pattern falls apart, play only D on every beat, then add the U before beat 3 and 4, one addition at a time.
messages.3006aa2cd413895a: Fingerpicking plays chord notes one at a time. Let the thumb p play string 4 (and sometimes 3), index i string 2 and middle m string 1. A simple pattern over one bar of 4/4 in eighths: p i m i p i m i. Hold the full chord shape so each note rings into the next.
messages.9d482c06053a0875: Without the left hand, play open strings p i m i p i m i slowly for four bars. Then hold C and play the pattern for two bars, then Am for two bars. Then C | Am | F | G7 with one bar each. Keep the thumb relaxed and the wrist still.
messages.12f67b9990e15cf9: Are the eight notes even, and does the chord keep ringing?
messages.a5c519bd9f3c88b9: If fingers tangle, practise only p i p i, then add m; say the finger names aloud in time.
messages.1bff4c8805422c17: From a chord chart to a song form
messages.77d79eeb5833bbcc: A chord chart lists chords per bar, often in sections such as verse and chorus. Repeat signs or written repeats tell you to play a section again. A short introduction (for example two bars of the first chord) and a clear ending (one strum on the last chord, let ring) make a performance feel complete.
messages.49b7deb87a05d4f3: Play this original chart with the lesson 20 strum: Intro C | C. Verse C | Am | F | G7 (twice). Chorus F | G7 | C | Am | F | G7 | C | C. End: one strum on C and let it ring. Count one silent bar before starting.
messages.e81f6cce3bcf6a77: Can I play through the sections without stopping at the joins?
messages.b3f7cf857e795d5a: If a join stops you, loop only the last bar of one section and the first bar of the next.
messages.2792f780434aa5fa: Map a chart and run your own practice cycle
messages.a61e6687c45c2aa6: Choose a chord chart you may use for yourself, or write your own with chords from this course. Map it: time signature, sections and repeats, every chord change, the hardest change, and a strum or picking pattern. A practice cycle then has four parts: a short warm-up (changes from lessons 18–19), work on the hardest change, one full play-through at a chosen tempo, and a written note.
messages.d1204d747c9b5ad5: Write the map, then run one cycle and note: tempo, the hardest change and what you observed (late / muted string / lost strum / no observed issue / uncertain). On another day repeat the same play-through at the same tempo and compare that change: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Write the next focus.
messages.d48f386498d8913e: Can I plan, run and compare a practice session without step-by-step help?
messages.87ca195fc12b2964: If the chart is too hard, keep two chords and one pattern; a short complete cycle still counts. A teacher can help with individual technique.
messages.b8177155a6849620: Review the identified high-G setup and external tuning check, 4→1 strings, fret/finger distinction, the C/Am/F/G7 diagrams and the G, Em, Dm and A7 shapes, 4/4 and 3/4 counts, down/up directions and strum patterns, ringing versus rests, a first fingerpicking pattern, tab decoding, the original study and a song-form chart. This is a bounded written beginner foundation, not all ukulele training, a grade qualification or sensor-confirmed mastery.
messages.f017bedab5f03ed6: On another day, locate strings/frets, decode the tab again, form the eight chords, play the study and the lesson 22 chart at a comfortable recorded tempo, and run one cycle with your own mapped chart (lesson 23). Use lesson 17’s same-task correction loop. Write what you can repeat, one uncertain outcome and its next practice lesson. Seek individual instruction for unresolved setup, discomfort or technique; there is no completion timer or score.
messages.644f90eb00820a3a: Identify the specified tuning and string/fret directions; read chord grids and a two-bar tab; form C/Am/F/G7 and G/Em/Dm/A7; count 4/4 and 3/4, use down/up strokes, a common strum pattern, counted rests and a first fingerpicking pattern; play an original eight-bar study and a song-form chart; then map your own chart and run a practice cycle comparing a specific correction at the same tempo. All performance checks are your own observation.
messages.6a5cc792bb808541: Natural notes in the first five frets
messages.479260283acc5f60: Natural notes are the letter names without sharps or flats. In sounding pitch, frets 0–5: string 4 E1 F1 (1) G1 (3) A1 (5); string 3 A1 B1 (2) C2 (3) D2 (5); string 2 D2 E2 (2) F2 (3) G2 (5); string 1 G2 A2 (2) B2 (4) C3 (5). Fret 5 on one string sounds the same as the next higher open string, for example string 4 fret 5 A1 = open string 3.
messages.905771132200fe40: Say and play the natural notes on string 4 from E1 to A1, then on string 3 from A1 to D2, one note per beat. Then find A1 in two places (string 4 fret 5 and open string 3) and D2 in two places, and compare that they sound the same. Keep index on fret 1–2 and ring/little finger on fret 4–5 as comfortable.
messages.97134f661677a4c5: Can I name any natural note in frets 0–5 and find one note in two places?
messages.7d125b50d7e52a10: If you lose track, recite the letters E F G A B C D on string 4 aloud while pointing, then play only the notes on frets 0, 3 and 5.
messages.7726337998015ba0: A major scale has the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. On bass a movable one-octave shape starting with finger 2 on the root covers three strings: root (2), 2nd (4), 3rd next string (1), 4th (2), 5th (4), 6th next string (1), 7th (3), octave (4). From C2 at string 3 fret 3 this gives C2 D2 E2 F2 G2 A2 B2 C3.
messages.872372d7fe2d68c1: Play the C major shape up and down: string 3 frets 3 5; string 2 frets 2 3 5; string 1 frets 2 4 5. One note per beat, alternating i and m, at a slow tempo. Then move the same shape so the root is G1 on string 4 fret 3 and play it again.
messages.76172bd35fabac7c: Can I play the shape evenly and say the scale degree of each note?
messages.f6f7c9f8cab96433: If the stretch from fret 2 to 5 is uncomfortable, shift the hand by one fret for the top notes instead of reaching; comfort comes before the textbook fingering.
messages.c4f3951be11252e3: Approach notes into a chord change
messages.cfb9dce10eab18ec: An approach note on the last beat of a bar leads into the next root. A chromatic approach is one fret below or above the target root; a scale approach is the scale note next to it. For C to F, play E2 (one fret below F2) on beat 4; for F to G, play F♯2 or A2. The approach is short and leads, it does not replace the root on beat 1.
messages.f01acba67d5f7938: Imagine the chart C | F | G | C. Play roots on beats 1–3 and an approach on beat 4: C2 C2 C2 E2 | F2 F2 F2 F♯2 | G2 G2 G2 B1 | C2 whole. Use string 3 fret 3 for C2, string 3 fret 2 for B1 and string 2 for F2 and G2. Count aloud; then try your own approach choices.
messages.3fafc981193b4a55: Does each approach lead clearly into the next root on beat 1?
messages.c0259cf960ef0dc1: If the change arrives late, play only beat 4 and the next beat 1 several times, keeping the left hand moving during beat 4.
messages.a2749d007119f1d9: A twelve-bar blues in A uses A7, D7 and E7 in the order A A A A | D D A A | E D A E. A common bass line plays root, third, fifth, sixth: over A that is A1 C♯2 E2 F♯2; over D it is D2 F♯2 A2 B2; over E it is E1 G♯1 B1 C♯2. Play them as quarter notes, one pattern per bar.
messages.0933ad266ff77ab2: Learn the A pattern first: open string 3, string 3 fret 4, string 2 fret 2, string 2 fret 4. Move it to D (open string 2, string 2 fret 4, string 1 fret 2, string 1 fret 4) and to E (open string 4, string 4 fret 4, string 3 fret 2, string 3 fret 4). Then play all twelve bars at a slow tempo with a counted bar before starting.
messages.343bd05539c32840: Can I keep track of where I am in the twelve bars without stopping?
messages.e72f94ca0779fd77: If you get lost, say the chord name on beat 1 of each bar while playing only roots, then add the pattern back one line of four bars at a time.
messages.6453f24eb93b5f55: Play with an external pulse and control note length
messages.5088744c7045ec18: A bassist keeps time for others. Use any external metronome or drum loop you already have; this course does not supply sound. Start slow enough that every note lands with the click. Note length is part of the groove: legato notes ring until the next one, staccato notes stop early with a gentle left-hand release or right-hand touch while the beat continues.
messages.c2bd8d1ba814fae4: Set a slow click. Play the lesson 21 blues roots as quarter notes, all legato for four bars, then all staccato for four bars. Then play half notes, ending each exactly on the next beat. Note your tempo and whether notes landed with the click: on time / early / late / uncertain.
messages.e45cdb6f1f3bfe27: Can I keep the click and choose short or long notes on purpose?
messages.3d8deb0b8630b2a8: If you drift from the click, play only on beat 1 of each bar and count the other beats silently, then add beats back.
messages.9aec76e7267d3f78: Write a bass line for a chart and run your own practice cycle
messages.3b12b025e56afddd: Choose a chord chart you may use for yourself, or write your own using chords from this course. Write a bass line: roots on beat 1, fifths or octaves on beat 3, and an approach note into each change. Map the hardest change and set a tempo. A practice cycle then has four parts: warm-up (lesson 19 scale), work on the hardest change, one play-through with an external pulse, and a written note.
messages.f44f21fc17d34567: Write your line for at least eight bars, then run one cycle and note: tempo, hardest change, observed result (late / wrong string / ringing through rest / buzz / no observed issue / uncertain). On another day repeat at the same tempo and compare that change: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Write the next focus.
messages.9e0b799851169b9b: Can I write, practise and compare a bass line without step-by-step help?
messages.6bee33cff61fa6b9: If the line is too busy, keep only roots on beat 1 and 3; a simple complete line is a valid result. A teacher can help with individual technique.

messages.fcf3228134d29847: Play any open string; the tuner guesses which one.

messages.a8c002965b633c5c: Matches the parts of the guitar and the six strings to their numbers and names.
messages.76a9ca07fc4f390d: Find the headstock with its tuning pegs, the neck and the body. Point to each part without turning a peg.
messages.95289db92d22062b: The nut is the small bar where the strings pass from the headstock onto the neck. The bridge holds them on the body. Metal fret wires cross the neck.
messages.598885d28741b8c7: Number the strings from the thinnest, string 1, to the thickest, string 6.
messages.2efe731bf86d89c7: Open strings from 6 to 1: E2, A2, D3, G3, B3, E4. The letter names the note; the number names its octave.
messages.9b7422703a4428a5: Choose a string number and name its open note. Then go the other way: choose a note and find its string.
messages.1c2c329f16cc87e0: No reference audio; the drill shows a guitar diagram.
messages.d98d2cff9d5d5379: Answer 8 questions on the diagram: tap the named part, or match a string number to its open note.
messages.786e098cfda3c7f2: Different answer: string 1 and string 6 swapped.
messages.ec6d1e5ebf8669a7: String 1 is the thinnest and highest-sounding string. Count from it toward string 6; do not count from the floor.
messages.c4c52b7748b173fe: Different answer: nut and fret wire swapped.
messages.a0c3c97917651b64: The nut is the one bar at the headstock end. All the other bars across the neck are fret wires.
messages.e05eff4a909989b4: Read the string map aloud and learn only two neighbouring strings first; add the rest one pair at a time.
messages.f85a46f0166eb07c: Sets up a supported sitting position, guitar angle and foot support, and holds it for 60 seconds.
messages.9a65bc8a5560a853: Sit on a chair without armrests, near the front edge. Keep both feet on the floor or one foot on a low support.
messages.285f0761614d7fc7: Let the guitar body rest on your leg and against your chest. Tilt the neck slightly upward.
messages.e2a056d2ef960850: Let go with both hands for a moment. If the guitar stays in place, your setup carries it, not your fretting hand.
messages.af434991d9b6c2ce: Put the phone to your side at chest height, about two metres away, with light in front of you, not behind.
messages.a16c25516c5db373: The camera asks for permission when this lesson starts. The image is processed on your phone; it is not saved and not sent.
messages.22a264d50cc7daab: The camera gives no score. It only shows a hint, and says "I can't see" when the image is not clear enough.
messages.95d81d7bddb52064: No reference audio; a side-view drawing shows the sitting position.
messages.fa8077c07c53b43b: Sit with the guitar in view of the camera and hold the position for 60 seconds. Follow any hint about your upper body or the guitar angle, then tick the checklist.
messages.b2a2c8dafbbe4131: Hold the position for 60 seconds and tick every checklist item. The camera only gives hints.
messages.c254faf40a81a055: Both feet were supported and my back was upright without strain.
messages.37f4dddf644789ad: The guitar stayed in place when I let go with both hands.
messages.2fa869092bcc5031: My shoulders and fretting hand stayed loose.
messages.35aceb62a75f8812: Hint: upper body leaning over the guitar.
messages.7782e750dd5e1d50: Tilt the guitar toward you a little instead of leaning over it to see the strings.
messages.932320bec6a74a5e: Move the phone back until your head, the guitar and your feet are in the frame, and turn on a light in front of you.
messages.e1e7ece0cafc3a03: Without a camera, use the checklist with a mirror. A strap or a guitar support is fine if it is more comfortable.
messages.cc804d11096f2ee5: Holds the pick loosely, places the fretting hand on the neck and names the fretting-hand finger numbers.
messages.7f6e003630434691: Hold the pick between the side of your index finger and the pad of your thumb. Let only a small tip show.
messages.b6050917acb90172: Fretting-hand fingers have numbers: index 1, middle 2, ring 3, little 4. The thumb has no number.
messages.363204bd71341bb7: Rest the thumb behind the neck, roughly behind finger 2. Curve the fingers so the fingertips meet the strings. Keep the wrist loose and close to straight, with a small gap between the neck and your palm.
messages.3d7a93225a3c9e19: If you play left-handed, the hands swap: the pick goes in your left hand and the right hand frets. The finger numbers stay the same.
messages.d9ab63cf70299de0: No reference audio; drawings show the pick grip and the fretting hand from the front.
messages.272d07e32c6a0ae4: Part 1: hold the pick and place the fretting hand on the neck in view of the camera for 30 seconds; follow any hint. Part 2: answer 6 questions on finger numbers.
messages.046fdf80c113fe55: Hold the hand position for 30 seconds and tick the checklist, then answer at least 5 of 6 questions. The camera only gives hints.
messages.6c42b561f1a00bf7: Only a small tip of the pick showed.
messages.aa22e042f0ba73f5: My thumb rested behind the neck, not over the top.
messages.60128016c12fd113: My fingertips, not the flat pads, touched the strings.
messages.55e79e01f2840d3c: Bring your elbow a little closer to your body and let the guitar neck point slightly upward.
messages.95e7bce0684d2304: Different answer: ring and little finger swapped.
messages.0e3cf59dbd106926: Count from the index finger: 1, 2, 3, 4. The little finger is always 4.
messages.5bf8fac0631b5afa: Bring the phone closer so both hands and the neck fill the frame, with light in front of you.
messages.1ae8629a39e805b6: Without a camera, use the checklist with a mirror. If a pick feels awkward, use the side of your thumb for now.
messages.b8dce171c35f0d42: Tunes the six strings to E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4 within 5 cents with the tuner.
messages.8566ef19a5490ac9: Standard tuning from string 6 to 1 is E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4. Check both the letter and the octave on the tuner.
messages.6c7ffc177cbec0cd: Follow one string up to the headstock with your finger to find its peg before you turn anything.
messages.bfdba8191ba1471e: Pluck the string softly and wait until the display is steady. Then turn the peg a little at a time.
messages.facaabbeb2c0ef17: If the note is low, tighten a little; if it is high, loosen past it and come back up to the note.
messages.bfd19b8338b51003: After the first round, check all six strings again. Tuning one string can move the others slightly.
messages.a7185283d0704d41: Each open-string target, E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4, played on demand, string-model synthesis.
messages.3841e3d615bec0dc: Tune the strings in order from 6 to 1. For each string, pluck it and adjust until the tuner holds steady within 5 cents for at least 1 second.
messages.75bd19046a6f2903: All six strings within 5 cents, each steady for at least 1 second.
messages.502b1b5df45d6c31: Different note: the string is more than 5 cents low.
messages.24d15c84027f3f41: Tighten the peg a very small amount, pluck again and wait for a steady display.
messages.f9132d2435450d93: Different note: an octave away from the target.
messages.c4774baea7bbfea6: Stop turning. Check that you are on the right peg and compare with the reference note; ask an experienced player if the string feels very tight or very loose.
messages.4c50e70948751da4: Pluck one string only, a little firmer, and keep the phone close to the guitar in a quiet room.
messages.f2a85e2b754ba77a: Tune only string 6 and string 1 first, then the four middle strings in a second short round.
messages.c3bebf10c28dbcdb: Compares two strings with the fifth-fret method and hears the beating when they differ.
messages.f7554d9c1f842909: Fret 5 on string 6 gives A2, the same note as open string 5. Two strings can check each other this way.
messages.362dc51d5bd6028e: Use fret 5 for the pairs 6–5, 5–4, 4–3 and 2–1. For the pair 3–2, use fret 4: string 3, fret 4 is B3.
messages.fdaaea525900778d: Play both notes together and listen. A slow wah-wah pulse, the beating, means they are slightly apart.
messages.8d135aaafa6e87fe: The closer the notes get, the slower the beating. When it disappears, the two strings match.
messages.6e3802b45c6213d7: Adjust only the open string of each pair. Your ear decides first; the tuner then checks.
messages.752456aa0d27d191: Two A2 notes played together: first matched, then 10 cents apart so the beating is clear; a drone on each target note on demand.
messages.bcbaf45c8d4d89ad: Go through the five string pairs. For each pair, play the fretted note and the open string together, adjust the open string until the beating stops, then let the tuner check it.
messages.cf159648b2e44e97: All five pairs within 10 cents of each other on the tuner.
messages.615f452393eb7562: I heard the beating before adjusting.
messages.bb00e9a5d08cd472: The beating slowed down and stopped as I turned the peg.
messages.057c809c0a1dff6d: I used fret 4 for the pair 3–2.
messages.23fbc7ac64c3fc0b: Different note: the open string is more than 10 cents low.
messages.bb1aeab2ac13cf40: Tighten the open string slowly while both notes ring; stop when the beating disappears.
messages.66e5a9ad8dd82d11: Different note: the pair 3–2 is a semitone apart.
messages.6fc5eabac2ae42fb: On string 3 use fret 4, not fret 5.
messages.ab8602c1e14711dd: Pluck both strings a little firmer and let them ring; keep the phone close to the guitar.
messages.48634f328c80d20e: Start with the pair 6–5 and the drone on A2 only; add one pair per session.
messages.186688553712cdbe: Plays one chosen open string cleanly and stops it on purpose without sounding its neighbours.
messages.80d8744f0eadb329: Use a pick or a bare fingertip. With a pick, hold it lightly and let only a small tip show.
messages.c5827c0560f27474: Pluck open string 1 with a small stroke. First listen as the sound fades on its own.
messages.47f169c68468a057: Play it again, then end the sound on purpose: touch only that string lightly with a free fingertip.
messages.5f67a81ada068987: Repeat on strings 2 and 3. Pause after each sound and listen for any neighbour that rang by accident.
messages.0de0706e4eb291bc: Keep the stroke small. A large stroke easily crosses several strings.
messages.64196ddc7165b537: Single open strings, each played and then stopped after two seconds, string-model synthesis.
messages.06073e39c6499452: The screen names 12 open strings in random order, from E2 to E4. Play each one cleanly, let it ring, then stop it before the next.
messages.43e9aae8d478be84: Only the chosen string rang each time.
messages.85a662ca9c84ad1c: I stopped each sound on purpose before the next one.
messages.151926fe6f46f334: Different note: the neighbouring string was heard.
messages.6536b53fc2f3a837: Make the stroke smaller and show less of the pick tip; find the string again and play slowly.
messages.04c776cc0612f801: Pluck a little firmer and check that no finger rests on the string.
messages.9adde16fed5b4482: Use only string 1 and one gentle stroke per try before adding two more strings.
messages.7d9772bdbe1cac38: Plays clean fretted notes by pressing close behind the fret with light pressure.
messages.a34f641263a63843: An open string is fret 0. From the nut toward the body, the first space is fret 1, then fret 2, then fret 3.
messages.f1ef82b7e567303f: Finger numbers are not fret numbers: index 1, middle 2, ring 3, little 4.
messages.1094cfdb197977ca: Place the fingertip just behind the fret wire, on the nut side. Pluck once and release.
messages.29034e2cda46738c: Ease the pressure slowly until the note goes fuzzy. Then add back only enough pressure for a clean note.
messages.9fe1c0305ce29c95: If a note buzzes, move closer to the fret before pressing harder. Release the hand between tries.
messages.b91fd7787a266da7: C4 and D4 on string 2, F4 and G4 on string 1, each held for two seconds, string-model synthesis.
messages.ca66d241bf7e90d9: Play 12 fretted notes as the screen shows them: C4 (string 2, fret 1), D4 (string 2, fret 3), F4 (string 1, fret 1) and G4 (string 1, fret 3). Take your time; there is no click.
messages.d3c177a09a1042af: I pressed just behind the fret, not on it or in the middle of the space.
messages.07db0b853fa87de9: The note is muffled. Move the fingertip closer to the fret and keep the finger curved so it does not touch the next string.
messages.842d699bdd15f125: The finger slid one fret up; recheck fret 1 and fret 3.
messages.ea646c23370be622: Use only C4 and F4 with finger 1 first. If pressing stays hard even close to the fret, have the guitar's setup checked instead of squeezing harder.
messages.52ea3c6251c57b2b: Starts practice with a short warm-up, takes planned breaks and stops when pain appears.
messages.78ae5fcf7d03a965: Begin each session with three easy minutes: slow notes, light pressure, loose shoulders.
messages.e6fa06f917affde0: Short and frequent beats long and rare. Take a break every 20–30 minutes; put the guitar down and shake out your hands.
messages.ff69494fc48fa8e6: Mild tenderness in the fingertips is common at the start. Sharp pain, numbness or tingling is a signal to stop for the day.
messages.5f9ebafca7423ec3: When your hand feels tired, slow down or stop. Speed can wait for the next session.
messages.a68d55581a48e931: Today's warm-up: frets 1-2-3-4 on string 1, one finger per fret, up and back down.
messages.421f23971e8cf33b: F4 F♯4 G4 G♯4 and back down, quarter notes at ♩=50 and ♩=40, string-model synthesis.
messages.5e62250bbd58b69a: Play the warm-up for 3 minutes at ♩=50: fingers 1-2-3-4 on frets 1 to 4 of string 1, then 4-3-2-1 back down. Stop at once if anything hurts.
messages.215455e3f34189ad: Complete the 3-minute warm-up. Notes are checked at the Level 1 default.
messages.d95510130176e764: I warmed up slowly with light pressure.
messages.5f19ba6935a3e6fb: I know when I will take my next break.
messages.505fe730f4ade6e7: I stopped if anything felt sharp or numb.
messages.e50896bf7284f084: Two fingers moved together. Keep finger 1 at fret 1 and give each fret its own finger.
messages.39988d44e7c6296b: Finger 4 may be landing on its pad. Curve it a little more and press just behind fret 4.
messages.9d8e94db5f0b8869: Use frets 1 to 3 with fingers 1 to 3 only, or play for 1 minute and rest for 1 minute.
messages.73153a0daf46e9ad: Reads string and fret from a TAB line and plays four bars on strings 6 and 5 at ♩=60.
messages.3bad7e341b718dc4: TAB has six lines, one per string. The top line is string 1, the thin high E; the bottom line is string 6.
messages.2311b421a10c12a9: A number on a line is the fret to press on that string. 0 means play the string open.
messages.5738452b93f2f6a7: Numbers are read left to right, like text. A number is not a finger number.
messages.2ffc5330210abbc4: TAB spacing does not show rhythm. Take the rhythm from the count above the TAB; here every note is one beat.
messages.b37b2996e2f5441d: Today's notes: string 6 open (E2) and fret 3 (G2), string 5 open (A2) and fret 3 (C3).
messages.e6a201ba5e58526f: The four-bar TAB line in quarter notes at ♩=60 and ♩=40, string-model synthesis.
messages.7164ef7ef6397b96: Read the four-bar TAB and play it along with the click, one note per beat. Start at ♩=50 and move up in steps of 5 to ♩=60.
messages.d31e8843400b8cda: I read the top TAB line as string 1.
messages.758967bbd3da9254: My line matched the reference at the slow tempo.
messages.a4a1164af4c34b67: Different note: string 1 was heard instead of string 6.
messages.322da35ecf9a95f4: TAB is upside down compared with how you look at the strings. Mark the top line "1, high E" and check one open string first.
messages.b1a690a332cafd71: Read one note ahead: while one note rings, find the next string and fret.
messages.337d125ba89cf808: Read only the open strings first (E2 and A2) at ♩=40, then add the fret-3 notes.
messages.bf5e24dc977901db: Plays E2, F2 and G2 on string 6 cleanly at ♩=60.
messages.c6152c604ed4a57a: String 6 is the thickest string and the lowest line of the TAB. Open, it sounds E2.
messages.accc694fc5559fea: Fret 1 is F2 with finger 1; fret 3 is G2 with finger 3. Keep finger 2 hovering over fret 2.
messages.a70cd6bfe6730ad0: Press just behind the fret wire, not on top of it and not in the middle of the space.
messages.20d6146214a4b365: Before the next note, lift the finger only enough to release the string; the open E then rings on its own.
messages.257da9cf55940c9c: E2 F2 G2 F2 E2 twice, at ♩=60 and at ♩=40, string-model synthesis.

messages.fc9c6686c5bd4218: I used finger 1 for F2 and finger 3 for G2.

messages.35fec58ce8b3115f: Drop to ♩=40 and loop only E2–G2 until both notes ring, then add F2.
messages.e1c979d3967621b3: Plays A2, B2 and C3 on string 5 cleanly at ♩=60.
messages.5b4381732f986a4d: String 5 is the second-thickest string and the second line from the bottom of the TAB. Open, it sounds A2.
messages.e2c6fc87857154fb: Fret 2 is B2 with finger 2; fret 3 is C3 with finger 3.
messages.84dc13ce65232472: Name each note before you play it: A, B, C, B.
messages.62c16c010738fd5c: When you move from string 6 to string 5, the picking hand moves too. Say the string change aloud and practise it on open strings first.
messages.aa1279f3ca985a5b: A2 B2 C3 B2 A2 twice, at ♩=60 and at ♩=40, string-model synthesis.

messages.7ee99f046aafb782: Plays D3, E3, F3 on string 4 and G3, A3 on string 3 in a two-bar line at ♩=60.
messages.41d957f83812aa04: String 4 open is D3. Fret 2 is E3 with finger 2; fret 3 is F3 with finger 3.
messages.e43a85c3d2e727a1: String 3 open is G3. Fret 2 is A3 with finger 2.

messages.cc9ef385891a4280: Then join them. Keep one steady beat through the string change; the change must not take extra time.
messages.b361f9b33b5d7313: D3 E3 F3 E3 | G3 A3 G3 D3 twice, at ♩=60 and at ♩=40, string-model synthesis.
messages.5d28d34993128118: Play the two-bar line twice along with the click. Start at ♩=50 and move up in steps of 5 to ♩=60.
messages.c2786015db571584: The string change did not break the beat.

messages.c3dcc281b460c162: Plays B3, C4, D4 on string 2 and E4, F4, G4 on string 1 in a two-bar line at ♩=60.
messages.553bbbc4804ff1f5: String 2 open is B3. Fret 1 is C4 with finger 1; fret 3 is D4 with finger 3.
messages.d7e346c350ba6215: String 1 open is E4. Fret 1 is F4 with finger 1; fret 3 is G4 with finger 3.
messages.dff4308a7586674f: Both strings use the same frets, 0-1-3. Only the string and the note names change.
messages.1cdeb55f0ecf347a: Use the open strings as anchors: B3 on string 2 and E4 on string 1. Count up from them to find the octave of each note.

messages.9c41de3412c0eced: Play strings 4 to 1 one by one at first; strum only when all four ring.
messages.3e09f5983209532c: Plays G cleanly on all six strings with a three- or four-finger shape.

messages.9ccc2e2c9335e28b: Build the three-finger G one finger at a time: finger 3 first, then finger 2, then finger 1. Strum only when all three are down.
messages.8a934280accc2dde: Plays C cleanly on five strings, with open G3 and E4 ringing.
messages.bd06b13c652407bf: C: x-3-2-0-1-0. Finger 3 on string 5, fret 3; finger 2 on string 4, fret 2; finger 1 on string 2, fret 1.

messages.bd7469b4de496aeb: Start the strum on string 5. String 6 is not played.
messages.9a37cc786d5b89fe: C spreads the hand over three frets. Let the thumb sit lower behind the neck instead of squeezing.
messages.10c1de3332be279c: C strummed once from string 5, then plucked string by string from 5 to 1, slowly.
messages.8c0bf1fcbc2c23f3: Strum C four times from string 5, in your own time. Then pluck the chord string by string; the app checks each string.
messages.a8ff374ce04ca062: Finger 2 on string 4 is leaning on string 3. Arch it so the open G rings.
messages.f007af58feb617f4: Finger 1 is flat. Stand it on its tip so string 1 is free.
messages.305dd599d074afc4: Play the small C (x-x-x-0-1-0, finger 1 only) first, then add fingers 2 and 3 one at a time.
messages.ca6f7554ac265edd: Changes between Em and Am at least 15 times in 60 seconds with every string ringing.

messages.662949369c1c312c: So fingers 2 and 3 move together, one string down, as one block. Then finger 1 drops onto string 2, fret 1.
messages.c4aee9018995b2e7: Lift the fingers only a little. A small move is a fast move.
messages.f344f2085fe0b048: Speed comes from repeating clean changes, not from rushing. A change that does not ring does not count.
messages.67e52f249236b620: Em and Am alternating, one strum each, at a slow and a moderate pace.
messages.753d8a9bd77938bc: Strum Em, then Am, once each. Change back and forth for 60 seconds. Each change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.b1c85ae9d4a6f197: At least 15 changes in 60 seconds. A change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.5ab50b4eeaa6e2ca: Fingers 2 and 3 moved together as one block.
messages.85923607b4185def: Your fingers lift too high. Keep them close to the strings and move the block in one motion.
messages.2b12e19e0dbda3dd: On Am, start the strum on string 5. Make the Am strum a little shorter.
messages.bfdcb82053911c73: Change without strumming for 30 seconds, looking at the fingers, then add the strum.
messages.7018945fa6cee024: Changes D–G and G–C at least 12 times each in 60 seconds with every string ringing.
messages.391b2b18c3b72104: D and G share no finger positions. Look at the new shape in your mind before you move.
messages.f9d27261703d414b: Lead with the bass finger. For G, aim finger 2 at string 6 first; for D, aim at the triangle on the top strings.
messages.fbbff75592513c42: G to C: fingers move one string down toward the floor. Finger 1 lands on string 2, fret 1.
messages.ffc5a9d99a6402c9: Move all fingers at the same time, close to the strings. Each chord starts its strum on its own bass string: D on 4, G on 6, C on 5.
messages.9b603e5dcab3c623: D and G alternating, then G and C alternating, one strum each, at a slow and a moderate pace.
messages.3fd08c16a405a9e4: Two sets. First D and G, then G and C. In each set, change back and forth for 60 seconds. Each change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.d2f87762871c5e9c: At least 12 changes in 60 seconds for each pair. A change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.fe8737e38e1aaa9a: All fingers moved at the same time.
messages.dccb9038bb63ca08: Each chord started on its own bass string.
messages.f5c77b9d76147d6a: The fingers land one by one. Practise placing all of them in one motion without strumming.
messages.ba03e44a94150ef5: On D, start the strum on string 4.
messages.f0e2ff8f9bda77a0: Use the three-finger G and practise one pair per session.
messages.da61ce5d605df9c0: Changes Am–E and C–Am at least 12 times each in 60 seconds, keeping shared fingers in place.
messages.d8e219d47a2484db: Am and E have the same finger shape. From Am, move the whole shape one string up toward your face, and you have E.
messages.b71fd29e0f6de71d: C and Am share two fingers: finger 1 on string 2, fret 1, and finger 2 on string 4, fret 2. Keep them down.
messages.b6fdc4c631b2773d: Between C and Am only finger 3 moves: string 5, fret 3 to string 3, fret 2.
messages.3efc764b61eac4e3: A finger that stays down is an anchor. It guides the hand and saves time.
messages.5ca87bcb35a39757: Am and E alternating, then C and Am alternating, one strum each, at a slow and a moderate pace.
messages.159b153e37230243: Two sets. First Am and E, then C and Am. In each set, change back and forth for 60 seconds. Each change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.83d93fc9cae3d787: Fingers 1 and 2 stayed down between C and Am.
messages.ac4c1e863b84d014: The whole shape moved together between Am and E.
messages.2b84d0e35b79f223: The anchor fingers are lifting. Keep fingers 1 and 2 touching the strings and move only finger 3.
messages.dfa277392f9e61ee: E uses string 6, but Am and C do not. After E, start the next strum on string 5.
messages.94d5082ceb619d89: Start with C–Am only; add Am–E in a later session.
messages.4cb77a28e64d19fe: Strums Em–Am–D–G in quarter-note downstrokes and changes chord on beat 1 at ♩=60.
messages.1926e1fb5e5709ae: Each chord gets one bar: four downstrokes, one on each click.
messages.4c91aa918f359c47: Beat 4 is your preparation time. Strum it lightly, or let it pass, and start moving the fingers.
messages.aad39f481d5e0c6f: The new chord must sound on beat 1. Being on time matters more than a perfect chord.
messages.6e0c112ae3ea00c5: Keep the strumming hand moving even if the fingers are late. Never stop the beat to fix a chord.
messages.6d7de328f83ddc66: Em, Am, D, G, one bar each in quarter-note downstrokes with a click, at ♩=60 and at ♩=45.
messages.d126df7638618fb9: Strum four downstrokes per chord with the click: Em, Am, D, G. Start at ♩=50 and move up in steps of 5 to ♩=60.
messages.d29326d643657e34: The new chord sounded on beat 1.
messages.61d1de3112936fb0: The change starts too late. Begin moving the fingers on beat 4.
messages.4a08d8ca2bce75db: The chord is landing in a hurry. Slow down one step and check the shape on beat 1.
messages.b9d4069f09f017cc: Give each chord two bars instead of one at ♩=45.
messages.3e1aab46ab35ae30: Plays the G–D–Em–C loop for eight bars in time at ♩=70.
messages.32c9f3ab0b4fec66: The loop is G, D, Em, C, one bar each, played twice. Strum four downstrokes per bar.
messages.2d913e1dc11e983d: Plan the preparation: use beat 4 of each bar to move to the next chord.
messages.95e9e9dda8de0e38: Practise the loop from another start too, for example from Em. Then no change depends on starting at G.
messages.cb802589a1409750: If a change is late, keep counting and land the next chord on beat 1. Do not restart.
messages.aa9b44f7bc5943ad: G–D–Em–C twice in quarter-note downstrokes over an original bass and drum loop, at ♩=70 and at ♩=50.
messages.588b299fe9ec62d7: Play the loop twice, eight bars, with the accompaniment. Start at ♩=60 and move up in steps of 5 to ♩=70; the checkpoint passes at ♩=70. Headphones help the microphone hear only your guitar.
messages.526c32373d3f6a50: One change is slower than the others. Loop just that pair, one bar before and one after, then rejoin the loop.
messages.4c4754bb3f4ec279: Use headphones for the accompaniment and keep the phone close to the guitar.
messages.916a4792a2ec6b0b: Give each chord two bars, making the loop sixteen bars, at ♩=60.
messages.1ba7430bfc61507a: Shows the Level 1 skills: tuning, single notes, open chords, chord changes in time and open strings by ear.
messages.1c60c46214e6e264: The test has five parts. Each part must pass on its own; passed parts are kept, so you only redo the rest.
messages.2ce7b0e0d0c5688c: Part 1, tuning: tune all six strings. Part 2, single notes: play a new eight-bar line on all strings at ♩=72.
messages.bc77c2e035e552d2: Part 3, chords: play Em, Am, E, A, D, G and C in order; each is checked string by string.
messages.c57cbf0c99bb85bd: Part 4, changes and rhythm: strum G–D–Em–C for eight bars in quarter notes at ♩=70 with the accompaniment.
messages.59d71493e934a8e8: Part 5, ear: listen to an open string and choose which string it is.
messages.5c9dfa1796123032: Every attempt uses new material, and you can take the parts in separate sessions.
messages.47558ba6d7dd26b3: Each new part-2 line once at ♩=72; the G–D–Em–C accompaniment loop at ♩=70; synthesized open strings E2 to E4 for part 5.
messages.795ed33c697b5fb1: Complete five parts. 1 Tuning: six strings. 2 Single notes: a new eight-bar line on all strings at ♩=72. 3 Chords: Em, Am, E, A, D, G, C in order, string by string. 4 Changes and rhythm: G–D–Em–C, eight bars of quarter-note strums at ♩=70. 5 Ear: 6 questions, which open string did you hear? Headphones help the microphone hear only your guitar.
messages.d444cd887d96ea8b: Each part passes on its own. Tuning: every string within 5 cents (within 20 cents while precise tuning is not ready). Single notes: Level 1 note and timing rules. Chords: at least 6 of 7 chords with every string heard. Changes and rhythm: Level 1 chord and timing rules. Ear: at least 5 of 6.
messages.642f85bd84589ece: Tune up from below: loosen a little past the note, then tighten slowly to it.
messages.6cf2c667f8015daf: Start each change on beat 4 so the new chord lands on beat 1.
messages.f3f817de716fdef4: For a part that did not pass, redo its module checkpoint, then retake only that part.
messages.04832a3ac1730fd3: Changes between Em and Am at least 20 times in 60 seconds and tracks the count over sessions.
messages.a015de0287b17ed3: A one-minute change is simple: strum one chord once, change, strum the next. The app counts every clean change.
messages.dd94a80a8db0ed11: Lift the fingers only a little above the strings; small moves are fast moves.
messages.f60ab3cd3a87af42: Look at the next chord's spot before you move, then move all fingers together.
messages.69c1c677905f4ba7: Em to Am: keep fingers 2 and 3 in the same shape and move them one string toward the floor. Then add finger 1 on string 2, fret 1.
messages.c3854bd9e3c45785: The app keeps your count for each chord pair. Repeat on later days and compare the numbers.
messages.dd7aba6721ea7b43: Em and Am, one strum each, changing every two beats at ♩=60, then at ♩=40.
messages.dcd03d729a466178: Change back and forth for 60 seconds. Each change counts when every string of the new chord is heard. Strum each chord once, then change.
messages.26891a2a610c9bb4: At least 20 changes in 60 seconds. A change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.b82fbe39634115fc: I strummed once per chord and changed without stopping.
messages.e1a88ca8342951b9: Lift the fingers less and look at the next spot first; aim for even changes, not fast ones.
messages.228c6623a9f1c8c6: Am starts on string 5. Aim the strum at string 5 and let string 6 stay silent.
messages.6b125a03f7c3a959: Strum a little firmer and keep the phone about one metre away.
messages.0ad2c2bfad6e99d1: Practise the move silently ten times, then try 30 seconds before the full minute.
messages.d5fe88bd01c8dbee: Changes between Am and C at least 18 times in 60 seconds without lifting the shared fingers.
messages.30c0d85d48b0515c: An anchor finger stays pressed on the same string and fret in both chords. It holds your hand in place.

messages.f13df3710e1e4d95: Only finger 3 travels: from string 3, fret 2 in Am to string 5, fret 3 in C.
messages.c9c3c00d133dbdbf: Am and C, one strum each, changing every two beats at ♩=60, then at ♩=40.

messages.3ac55cc081bf7b03: At least 18 changes in 60 seconds. A change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.8766639e962bf8aa: Fingers 1 and 2 stayed on the strings during every change.
messages.73abfc05f24e6f47: In C, finger 2 leans on open string 3. Arch the finger and press with the tip.
messages.24a5814a1012b679: Move only finger 3 back and forth without strumming, then add the strum and try 30 seconds.
messages.6247b6939e72ed4e: Changes between A and D at least 18 times in 60 seconds with a guide finger.
messages.491a3f9bb9ce274f: A is x-0-2-2-2-0 with fingers 1, 2 and 3 on strings 4, 3 and 2. D is x-x-0-2-3-2.

messages.0bafda1ec9830852: A starts on string 5, D on string 4. Make the strum smaller for D.
messages.78a5933141587819: A and D, one strum each, changing every two beats at ♩=60, then at ♩=40.
messages.22afc9b447f28753: Change back and forth for 60 seconds. Each change counts when every string of the new chord is heard. Keep finger 3 on string 2 the whole time.
messages.999da403bfc64ba6: Finger 3 slid along string 2 without lifting.
messages.28e79e2c705d3fe5: D starts on string 4. Aim the strum at string 4 and keep the stroke short.
messages.46327296b55746b9: In A, three fingers crowd fret 2 and touch string 1. Angle the fingers slightly and keep the tips up.
messages.fca96e68572a0574: Changes between D and G at least 18 times in 60 seconds.
messages.472480204eea1546: D is x-x-0-2-3-2. G is 3-2-0-0-0-3, or 3-2-0-0-3-3 with four fingers.
messages.18c6a0552a792ca2: With the four-finger G, finger 3 stays on string 2, fret 3 as an anchor. Fingers 2, 1 and 4 move around it.

messages.d014f3376f5e6de8: Play G (3-2-0-0-0-3) with finger 3 on string 6, finger 2 on string 5 and finger 4 on string 1.
messages.a0ee619043299b88: To reach C (x-3-2-0-1-0), move fingers 3 and 2 together one string toward the floor. Then drop finger 1 on string 2, fret 1.
messages.7aed99d125e6b713: Keep the shape of fingers 3 and 2 during the move, like one block.

messages.4122cede4f982ada: At least 16 changes in 60 seconds. A change counts when every string of the new chord is heard.
messages.7e5fcdfa7f8b050c: Fingers 3 and 2 moved together as one block.
messages.0eb93ae49009e061: C starts on string 5. Aim the strum at string 5 and let string 6 stay silent.

messages.6bb4b15b5e99cede: E is 0-2-2-1-0-0 and A is x-0-2-2-2-0. Both shapes sit mostly on fret 2.
messages.4e0cbad6e55bc169: Keep your hand at the same place on the neck. Only the fingers change strings.

messages.90e5c1ac3cfa69a6: E starts on string 6, A on string 5. Make the strum a little smaller for A.

messages.01d093652bb336a4: A starts on string 5. Aim the strum at string 5 and let string 6 stay silent.
messages.33873302ef18c556: In E, finger 1 on string 3 lands late. Place it together with the other two fingers.
messages.529bd44513ee49d8: Plays Dm cleanly string by string and changes between Dm and Am at least 15 times in 60 seconds.
messages.c57989819966d747: Dm is x-x-0-2-3-1: finger 2 on string 3, fret 2, finger 3 on string 2, fret 3, finger 1 on string 1, fret 1.

messages.ff7ab0b2cfda0ee8: Plays an 8-bar I–IV–V progression in G with the accompaniment at ♩=70.

messages.042e974ce4aae520: Chord I feels like home. Chord V pulls back to it; listen for that pull from D to G.
messages.d86563d2fecb94b9: You already know these changes. Prepare each one on beat 4.

messages.9b4cd8b4792ffff2: Neighbouring letters are not always a whole step apart. E–F and B–C are half steps; all other natural neighbours are whole steps.

messages.0ab44640d26b3d2b: Later, the same counting finds larger steps: three frets is a minor third, five frets a perfect fourth.

messages.d4e785e9620ce715: Complete four parts. 1 Pulse: 8 claps each at ♩=60, 80 and 100, plus a four-bar rhythm at ♩=70. 2 Pitch: 10 questions on high or low and contour, plus 6 notes sung back in your own octave, or the on-screen 'Same or different?' set instead. 3 Rhythm reading: 4 new two-bar lines at ♩=70. 4 Note reading: 20 notes from both clefs.

messages.a4ba7331ccdcafd2: If the thumb or wrist feels strained, release the hand and rest before the next set.
